readerTitle: A creator wants $3,000 to post about your app. Is it worth it?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (청소 예약 앱, 식당 전문 회계 사무소) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 크리에이터 광고는 조회수가 아니라 '영상이 없었으면 오지 않았을 고객 한 명에 얼마를 냈는가'로 판단하고, 한 명에서 통했다고 스무 명으로 늘리기 전에 다시 잰다.
misconception: 팔로워가 많고 할인 코드 사용자가 많으면 크리에이터 광고가 성공한 것이고, 잘 된 한 건을 그대로 여러 명에게 늘리면 된다.

sources.text: 마케팅의 표준 개념 (고객 획득 비용, 증분 효과 측정, 수확 체감)

factChecks.note: 코드 기준 고객당 비용: $3,000 ÷ 60명 = $50. 고객 가치: 예약당 앱이 남기는 $20 × 첫해 예약 4회 = $80. 모두 가상 수치입니다.
증분 계산: 평소 주간 첫 예약 30건, 영상 주간 75건 → 추가 45건. $3,000 ÷ 45 = $66.67(카드에는 약 $67). 코드 사용 60명 중 약 15명은 영상 없이도 왔을 고객이라는 해석입니다.
차트 수치(크리에이터 1: $67, 2~3: $85, 4~6: $120)는 수확 체감을 보여주기 위한 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: A creator wants $3,000 to post about your app.
body: You run an app that books home cleaners in one city. A home-tips creator with 400,000 followers offers a 60-second video about you for $3,000.
Her videos get huge views. Your team is excited. The question is what those views are worth to you.

image.label: A phone showing a cleaning video with a price tag beside it
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 스마트폰 화면에 깔끔한 거실을 청소하는 짧은 영상, 옆에 "$3,000" 가격표가 매달려 있음. 화면 위로 하트와 조회수 아이콘이 떠오름. 실제 SNS 로고나 앱 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What do you do with the offer?
body: Each customer books about four cleanings in their first year. You keep about $20 per booking after paying the cleaner and fees.

options.text: Accept. At 400,000 followers, it's under a cent per viewer
options.feedback: Cheap views are not cheap customers. **Paying for customers** means comparing the cost of each booked customer with what that customer leaves you.

options.text: Run one video with its own code, then compare the cost per customer with the $80 a customer is worth
options.feedback: This is **paying for customers** in action. You risk $3,000 once and learn what a customer from her audience actually costs.

options.text: Decline. Creators work for fashion brands, not cleaning apps
options.feedback: Caution saves the $3,000, but it's a guess. A small test answers the question for less than the cost of being wrong.

cards.title: The video goes out. The code gets used.
body: By the code alone, each customer cost $50 and is worth $80. A clear win. Or is it?

cards.title: Did the video bring all 60?
body: Some codes ended up on a coupon website. A few code users had already downloaded the app weeks ago. How do you count what the video did?

options.text: Count all 60. They used her code
options.feedback: A code shows who used it, not who came because of it. People who would have booked anyway grab any discount they find.

options.text: Compare first bookings that week with a normal week in the same city
options.feedback: This asks **did marketing cause the sale**. Only the bookings above your normal level were truly added by the video.

options.text: Count app downloads during the video week
options.feedback: Downloads show interest, but a download is not a paying customer. You'd still need to see who booked.

cards.title: The real cost was $67, not $50.
body: A normal week brings about 30 first bookings in that city. The video week brought 75. So the video added about **45 customers**, not 60.
About 15 code users would have come anyway. They just got a discount on the way.
$3,000 ÷ 45 = about $67 per added customer. Still below the $80 a customer is worth, but the margin is much thinner than the code suggested.

image.label: Two weekly bars: 30 normal bookings vs 75 in the video week
image.brief: 막대 두 개 비교. 왼쪽 "Normal week 30", 오른쪽 "Video week 75". 오른쪽 막대에서 위쪽 45칸만 밝은 색으로 "Added by the video" 라벨, 아래 30칸은 회색. 로고 없음.

cards.title: The next creators cost more per customer.
body: Encouraged, you pay five more creators. Each new one reaches a smaller or overlapping audience. Many viewers already saw the first video.
This is **diminishing returns**: each extra dollar buys fewer new customers than the last.
cards.callout: By creators 4–6, you pay $120 for a customer worth $80.

cards.title: Your $80 is still a forecast.
body: The $80 assumes four bookings in the first year. Customers who came for a discount may book once and leave. Check whether creator customers rebook as often as your others before you trust the math.
One week in one city is also a small sample. A rainy week or a holiday can move your normal level. Repeat the test before you sign a long deal.

cards.title: Now it's a bookkeeping firm.
body: Your firm does bookkeeping for restaurants. Each new client leaves about $3,000 a year after staff time. A popular restaurant-industry newsletter offers a sponsored issue for $2,000, or 12 issues for $18,000.

options.feedback: The discount locks you in before you know the cost per client. **Diminishing returns** means issue 12 likely brings fewer clients than issue one.

options.text: Buy one issue with its own booking link, compare inquiries with a normal month, then decide
options.feedback: You measure **cost per added client** and check what the issue actually caused. If one client signs, the $2,000 is already covered.

options.text: Decide by the newsletter's 50% open rate
options.feedback: A high open rate means attention, which matters. But you pay for clients, not readers, so measure who books a call.

cards.title: Pay creators for customers they truly add.
body: This lesson used three ideas: **paying for customers** (cost vs value), **did marketing cause the sale** (count only what's above normal), and **diminishing returns** (the next dollar buys less).
**Try it today:** pick one marketing channel you pay for. Compare last month's customers with a month when you didn't spend on it.
